questions.stem: This graph compares blood oxygen content curves for normal blood, anemia (Hb 7 g/dL), and blood with 50% carboxyhemoglobin. Compared with normal blood, how does carbon monoxide (dashed curve) affect oxygen transport?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CO both lowers total O2-carrying capacity and left-shifts the dissociation curve

choices.label: B
choices.text: CO increases oxygen content but right-shifts the curve, improving delivery

choices.label: C
choices.text: CO lowers content but right-shifts the curve, aiding unloading

choices.label: D
choices.text: CO only lowers dissolved oxygen without affecting hemoglobin

choices.label: E
choices.text: CO raises the P50 so tissues extract more oxygen

explanation.summary: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with high affinity, reducing available O2 binding sites (lower content) and simultaneously left-shifting the curve for the remaining sites, so oxygen is held more tightly and released poorly at tissues, causing profound hypoxia despite a 'normal' PaO2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with high affinity, reducing available O2 binding sites (lower content) and simultaneously left-shifting the curve for the remaining sites, so oxygen is held more tightly and released poorly at tissues, causing profound hypoxia despite a 'normal' PaO2.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CO lowers, not raises, oxygen content by occupying heme sites, and it shifts the remaining curve left, which impairs rather than improves delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The reduced content is correct, but the shift is to the left, not the right, so unloading at tissues is hindered rather than aided.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dissolved O2 depends on PaO2, which stays normal in CO poisoning; the harm comes from CO occupying hemoglobin binding sites.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CO lowers the P50 (left shift), increasing hemoglobin's affinity for the remaining O2, so tissues extract less oxygen, not more.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with a 3-month history of cough and weight loss has the hand finding shown. This finding is most commonly associated with which category of disease?

explanation.summary: Digital clubbing reflects distal phalangeal soft-tissue proliferation and loss of the Lovibond angle; it is strongly linked to chronic hypoxemia and intrathoracic disease such as lung malignancy, bronchiectasis, and pulmonary fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Digital clubbing reflects distal phalangeal soft-tissue proliferation and loss of the Lovibond angle; it is strongly linked to chronic hypoxemia and intrathoracic disease such as lung malignancy, bronchiectasis, and pulmonary fibrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute viral upper respiratory infections are brief and self-limited, far too short to produce chronic soft-tissue proliferation of the nail bed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve numbness and thenar atrophy, not changes in the distal phalanges or nails.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Iron deficiency causes spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia), not clubbing with loss of the Lovibond angle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Osteoarthritis produces bony Heberden and Bouchard nodes at the interphalangeal joints, not bulbous fingertip enlargement with loss of the nail angle.

questions.stem: This bronchial biopsy is from a 55-year-old man who has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 30 years. What change is shown at the arrow?

explanation.summary: Chronic irritation from cigarette smoke drives replacement of the delicate respiratory epithelium by more resistant stratified squamous epithelium, a reversible adaptive metaplasia. It compromises mucociliary clearance and can be a precursor field for dysplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic irritation from cigarette smoke drives replacement of the delicate respiratory epithelium by more resistant stratified squamous epithelium, a reversible adaptive metaplasia. It compromises mucociliary clearance and can be a precursor field for dysplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anaplasia is the complete loss of differentiation seen in malignant tumors, not an adaptive change to a mature cell type.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypertrophy is enlargement of existing cells without changing cell type; here the columnar epithelium has been replaced by a different type.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Goblet cell hyperplasia increases mucus-secreting cells within the columnar epithelium; the epithelium shown is flat and stratified.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dysplasia implies disordered maturation with nuclear atypia and loss of polarity; orderly stratified squamous replacement is metaplasia.

questions.stem: These two lung sections are shown at the same magnification; panel B is normal lung for comparison. A 64-year-old long-time smoker has progressive dyspnea and hyperinflated lungs. What does panel A show?

explanation.summary: Panel A shows permanently enlarged airspaces with destroyed, thinned septa compared with the normal alveolar architecture in panel B. This is emphysema: enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with alveolar wall destruction, which reduces gas-exchange surface area.
explanation.whyCorrect: Panel A shows permanently enlarged airspaces with destroyed, thinned septa compared with the normal alveolar architecture in panel B. This is emphysema: enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with alveolar wall destruction, which reduces gas-exchange surface area.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage fills alveoli with red cells and hemosiderin-laden macrophages, without destruction of septa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Organizing pneumonia shows plugs of loose fibroblastic tissue (Masson bodies) within airspaces, not enlarged empty airspaces.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alveolar proteinosis fills alveoli with PAS-positive granular surfactant material, preserving the alveolar architecture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary edema fills alveoli with pink proteinaceous fluid while septa remain intact, rather than enlarging airspaces with destroyed walls.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history has progressive exertional dyspnea. His PA chest radiograph is shown. These findings are most typical of which condition?

explanation.summary: In emphysema, air trapping expands lung volumes, flattening the diaphragms, increasing lung lucency, widening the retrosternal space, and narrowing the heart shadow. These are the classic radiographic signs of COPD hyperinflation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In emphysema, air trapping expands lung volumes, flattening the diaphragms, increasing lung lucency, widening the retrosternal space, and narrowing the heart shadow. These are the classic radiographic signs of COPD hyperinflation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiogenic edema shows cardiomegaly, vascular redistribution, interstitial lines, and effusions, not hyperlucent lungs with a narrow heart.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A large pleural effusion causes a dense opacity with a meniscus, blunting costophrenic angles, rather than hyperlucency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lobar pneumonia shows a dense lobar consolidation with air bronchograms, not bilateral hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tension pneumothorax shows a unilateral lucent hemithorax without lung markings and mediastinal shift away from the affected side.

questions.stem: This H&E section of a bronchus is from a 24-year-old woman who died during a prolonged episode of severe wheezing. The arrows mark key features. What is the diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Basement membrane thickening, smooth muscle hypertrophy, goblet-cell/mucous hyperplasia, and eosinophilic inflammation are the histologic hallmarks of chronic asthmatic airway remodeling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Basement membrane thickening, smooth muscle hypertrophy, goblet-cell/mucous hyperplasia, and eosinophilic inflammation are the histologic hallmarks of chronic asthmatic airway remodeling.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bronchiectasis shows permanently dilated bronchi with destroyed walls and purulent mucus, not hypertrophied smooth muscle with eosinophilic infiltrates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic bronchitis shows submucosal gland hypertrophy (raised Reid index) with neutrophil-predominant inflammation, not eosinophil-rich infiltrates and basement membrane thickening.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls distal to the terminal bronchiole; it does not remodel the bronchial wall with a thick basement membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tuberculosis forms caseating granulomas with epithelioid macrophages and Langhans giant cells, not eosinophilic airway remodeling.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a chronic cough productive of large volumes of foul sputum and recurrent pneumonias. Her chest CT is shown (arrows). What condition does this represent?

explanation.summary: Clusters of abnormally dilated bronchi forming cystic and string-of-beads patterns on HRCT are diagnostic of bronchiectasis, reflecting irreversible bronchial wall destruction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Clusters of abnormally dilated bronchi forming cystic and string-of-beads patterns on HRCT are diagnostic of bronchiectasis, reflecting irreversible bronchial wall destruction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Centrilobular emphysema shows low-attenuation areas without visible walls around a central artery, not thick-walled dilated bronchi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A lung abscess is a single thick-walled cavity, often with an air-fluid level, rather than a cluster of dilated tubular airways.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A pleural effusion is dependent fluid density in the pleural space outside the lung, not within clustered airways.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary embolism is seen as filling defects within contrast-enhanced pulmonary arteries, not as cystic airway changes.

questions.stem: This lung was removed at transplant from a 22-year-old with lifelong recurrent Pseudomonas infections and pancreatic insufficiency. What structural airway disease is shown?

explanation.summary: Recurrent infection and mucus plugging in CF cause permanent, abnormal dilation of bronchi, seen grossly as the enlarged, pus-filled cystic airway spaces characteristic of bronchiectasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recurrent infection and mucus plugging in CF cause permanent, abnormal dilation of bronchi, seen grossly as the enlarged, pus-filled cystic airway spaces characteristic of bronchiectasis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alveolar hemorrhage gives a diffusely red, blood-filled parenchyma without dilated, pus-filled cystic airways.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Emphysema enlarges thin-walled distal airspaces and is not filled with purulent material from dilated bronchi.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lobar pneumonia consolidates a lobe uniformly without permanent dilation of the bronchi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A pulmonary infarct is a wedge-shaped hemorrhagic area based on the pleura, not diffuse dilated cystic airways.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old unvaccinated child has fever, drooling, and muffled voice. Lateral neck radiographs are shown (left, a normal child for comparison; right, this patient). What is the most likely diagnosis and cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute epiglottitis - Haemophilus influenzae type b

explanation.summary: The 'thumbprint sign' on a lateral neck film is a swollen epiglottis, characteristic of acute epiglottitis, classically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (now less common with Hib vaccination). It is an airway emergency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 'thumbprint sign' on a lateral neck film is a swollen epiglottis, characteristic of acute epiglottitis, classically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b (now less common with Hib vaccination). It is an airway emergency.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A radiopaque foreign body appears as a discrete dense object in the airway or esophagus, not as a swollen epiglottis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Croup's steeple sign is subglottic tracheal narrowing on a frontal film; the epiglottis is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peritonsillar abscess is diagnosed clinically by uvular deviation and trismus; it does not produce a thumb sign on a lateral neck film.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retropharyngeal abscess widens the prevertebral soft tissues on the lateral film rather than enlarging the epiglottis.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old unvaccinated child has sore throat, fever, and a gray membrane over the tonsils. A Gram stain of the throat swab is shown. Which organism is most likely?

explanation.summary: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a Gram-positive, club-shaped bacillus that divides to form V- and Y-shaped 'Chinese letter' arrangements. Its exotoxin (ADP-ribosylates EF-2) causes the pseudomembranous pharyngitis and systemic toxicity of diphtheria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a Gram-positive, club-shaped bacillus that divides to form V- and Y-shaped 'Chinese letter' arrangements. Its exotoxin (ADP-ribosylates EF-2) causes the pseudomembranous pharyngitis and systemic toxicity of diphtheria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Actinomyces is a Gram-positive branching filamentous rod forming sulfur granules, not club-shaped rods in Chinese-letter clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacillus anthracis forms large boxcar-shaped Gram-positive rods in long chains (bamboo-stick appearance).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Clostridium tetani is a Gram-positive rod with a terminal spore giving a drumstick or tennis-racket shape.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Listeria is a short Gram-positive rod with tumbling motility, without club shapes or V/Y palisades.

questions.stem: A throat-swab isolate from a child with a gray adherent pharyngeal membrane is stained with a special stain, shown here. What are the dark structures at the ends of the rods?

explanation.summary: Corynebacterium diphtheriae stores polyphosphate as metachromatic (Babes-Ernst/volutin) granules that stain a contrasting color at the cell poles with stains such as Albert or Neisser, aiding presumptive identification.
explanation.whyCorrect: Corynebacterium diphtheriae stores polyphosphate as metachromatic (Babes-Ernst/volutin) granules that stain a contrasting color at the cell poles with stains such as Albert or Neisser, aiding presumptive identification.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capsules appear as clear halos around organisms with negative staining or quellung, not as dark polar granules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycogen does not stain as metachromatic polar granules, and C. diphtheriae is identified by its polyphosphate stores.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sulfur granules are macroscopic yellow colonies of Actinomyces found in draining pus, not intracellular polar granules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Corynebacterium does not form spores; terminal endospores are features of Clostridium and Bacillus.

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 9-year-old has sore throat, low-grade fever, and cervical lymphadenopathy. His oropharynx is shown. What is this lesion?

explanation.summary: The diphtheritic pseudomembrane is a tough, adherent gray coagulum of fibrin, necrotic epithelium, leukocytes, and bacteria. It bleeds on removal and can extend to obstruct the airway, a hallmark of respiratory diphtheria.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diphtheritic pseudomembrane is a tough, adherent gray coagulum of fibrin, necrotic epithelium, leukocytes, and bacteria. It bleeds on removal and can extend to obstruct the airway, a hallmark of respiratory diphtheria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aphthous ulcers are small, shallow, painful ulcers with a gray-yellow base and red halo, not a confluent bleeding pharyngeal membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Herpetic gingivostomatitis causes painful clustered vesicles and ulcers on the gums and lips, not an adherent gray membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukoplakia is a white patch on oral mucosa that cannot be scraped off, usually on the tongue or buccal mucosa, and is premalignant rather than infectious.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrush forms creamy white plaques that scrape off easily, leaving a red base, rather than a tough gray membrane.

questions.stem: These H&E sections are from a lung biopsy of a 68-year-old man with progressive dyspnea and bibasilar crackles; the arrow marks a key feature. Which histologic pattern is depicted?

explanation.summary: Spatially heterogeneous fibrosis with microscopic honeycombing defines the UIP pattern of IPF. NSIP is uniform, DAD shows hyaline membranes, and organizing pneumonia shows intraluminal fibroblastic plugs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spatially heterogeneous fibrosis with microscopic honeycombing defines the UIP pattern of IPF. NSIP is uniform, DAD shows hyaline membranes, and organizing pneumonia shows intraluminal fibroblastic plugs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diffuse alveolar damage shows hyaline membranes lining alveoli in the acute phase, not chronic patchy collagen with honeycombing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NSIP shows uniform, temporally homogeneous interstitial inflammation or fibrosis, without honeycomb cysts and patchy heterogeneity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Organizing pneumonia shows intraluminal plugs of loose fibroblastic tissue (Masson bodies), with preserved architecture.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Respiratory bronchiolitis shows pigmented smoker's macrophages in respiratory bronchioles, without dense fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has 2 years of progressive dyspnea, dry cough, and bibasilar 'velcro' crackles. His high-resolution chest CT is shown. This imaging pattern is most specific for which of the following?

explanation.summary: Subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis defines the UIP pattern, the radiologic hallmark of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other fibrotic interstitial lung diseases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Subpleural, basal-predominant reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis defines the UIP pattern, the radiologic hallmark of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and other fibrotic interstitial lung diseases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Centrilobular emphysema shows upper-lobe low-attenuation areas without walls, not basal reticulation with clustered thick-walled cysts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage causes patchy or diffuse ground-glass and consolidation without fibrotic honeycombing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ground-glass opacity alone reflects active inflammation without fibrosis; honeycombing indicates established fibrotic disease of the UIP type.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lymphangitic carcinomatosis causes nodular, beaded interlobular septal thickening, often with effusions, rather than subpleural honeycombing.

questions.stem: This cut surface of a lung is from a 72-year-old man who died of progressive restrictive lung disease. What is this end-stage gross finding called?

explanation.summary: End-stage fibrosis destroys normal architecture, leaving thick fibrous bands enclosing dilated airspaces, grossly termed honeycomb lung. The distractors produce localized or thin-walled cavities rather than diffuse fibrotic remodeling.
explanation.whyCorrect: End-stage fibrosis destroys normal architecture, leaving thick fibrous bands enclosing dilated airspaces, grossly termed honeycomb lung. The distractors produce localized or thin-walled cavities rather than diffuse fibrotic remodeling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cavitary tuberculosis creates localized apical cavities with caseous necrosis rather than diffuse fibrous walls around many cysts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cystic bronchiectasis shows dilated bronchi in continuity with the airway tree, often containing pus, rather than diffuse fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bullae are thin-walled, air-filled spaces larger than 1 cm from emphysema, not cysts enclosed by dense fibrous tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abscesses are discrete cavities filled with pus and necrotic debris, not uniform cysts set within dense fibrosis.

questions.stem: This lung biopsy (left, H&E; right, polarized view) is from a 58-year-old sandblaster with progressive dyspnea. What is the lesion on the left?

explanation.summary: The silicotic nodule is characterized by concentric ('onion-skin') layers of hyalinized collagen. Polarized light reveals birefringent silica particles within it. These nodules coalesce over time and can progress to massive fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The silicotic nodule is characterized by concentric ('onion-skin') layers of hyalinized collagen. Polarized light reveals birefringent silica particles within it. These nodules coalesce over time and can progress to massive fibrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchogenic carcinoma shows infiltrating malignant epithelial cells rather than an acellular whorl of hyalinized collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TB granulomas have central caseous necrosis surrounded by epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans giant cells, not layered collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A hamartoma contains a disorganized mix of cartilage, fat, and smooth muscle, often with popcorn calcification, not whorled collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Caplan nodules occur in pneumoconiosis with rheumatoid arthritis and have central necrosis with palisading histiocytes, not purely concentric hyalinized collagen.

questions.stem: This lung biopsy is from a 70-year-old retired shipyard worker with progressive dyspnea. What are the golden-brown rod-shaped structures?

explanation.summary: Asbestos bodies are ferruginous bodies: thin asbestos fibers coated with an iron-containing proteinaceous material, producing golden-brown beaded rods with knobbed ends. Their presence indicates significant asbestos exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Asbestos bodies are ferruginous bodies: thin asbestos fibers coated with an iron-containing proteinaceous material, producing golden-brown beaded rods with knobbed ends. Their presence indicates significant asbestos exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Charcot-Leyden crystals are slender, bipyramidal crystals from eosinophil galectin-10 in asthma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Curschmann spirals are coiled mucus casts from small bronchioles in asthma, not iron-coated beaded rods.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Psammoma bodies are round, concentrically laminated calcifications in papillary tumors like thyroid and ovarian carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Schaumann bodies are laminated calcium-protein concretions inside giant cells in sarcoidosis, round rather than dumbbell-shaped.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has hemoptysis and acute kidney injury with hematuria. A lung biopsy is shown. What process is depicted?

explanation.summary: Filling of intact alveoli with red blood cells indicates alveolar hemorrhage, a manifestation of pulmonary capillaritis seen in autoimmune conditions such as anti-GBM disease and ANCA-associated vasculitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Filling of intact alveoli with red blood cells indicates alveolar hemorrhage, a manifestation of pulmonary capillaritis seen in autoimmune conditions such as anti-GBM disease and ANCA-associated vasculitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alveolar proteinosis fills alveoli with granular, PAS-positive pink material, not red blood cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bronchopneumonia fills airspaces with neutrophils, centered on bronchioles, rather than red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Emphysema leaves enlarged, empty airspaces with destroyed septa, while here the septa are intact and the spaces are filled.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transudative edema fills alveoli with pale, homogeneous pink fluid with few cells, not packed erythrocytes.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man has hemoptysis and rapidly rising creatinine. Direct immunofluorescence of his renal biopsy, stained for IgG, is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A continuous linear IF pattern reflects antibodies bound uniformly to the GBM (anti-collagen IV), the defining feature of anti-GBM disease, which also targets the alveolar basement membrane to cause pulmonary hemorrhage.
explanation.whyCorrect: A continuous linear IF pattern reflects antibodies bound uniformly to the GBM (anti-collagen IV), the defining feature of anti-GBM disease, which also targets the alveolar basement membrane to cause pulmonary hemorrhage.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IgA nephropathy shows mesangial IgA deposits, not linear staining along the GBM.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Membranous nephropathy shows fine granular subepithelial IgG deposits along the capillary loops and presents with nephrotic syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Minimal change disease is negative on immunofluorescence, with only podocyte effacement on electron microscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Post-streptococcal GN shows coarse, granular lumpy-bumpy deposits with subepithelial humps, not a smooth linear pattern, and does not cause lung hemorrhage.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has dyspnea and dullness to percussion at the right lung base. His chest radiographs before and after treatment are shown; the arrow marks the abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Fluid in the pleural space (pleural effusion) is dense and layers dependently, producing a white opacity that blunts the costophrenic angle. Drainage or treatment restores the normal dark, air-filled lung seen post-treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluid in the pleural space (pleural effusion) is dense and layers dependently, producing a white opacity that blunts the costophrenic angle. Drainage or treatment restores the normal dark, air-filled lung seen post-treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiomegaly enlarges the central cardiac silhouette and does not blunt one costophrenic angle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lobar consolidation follows lobar anatomy with air bronchograms and does not characteristically blunt the costophrenic angle with a meniscus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrosis produces bilateral reticular opacities and volume loss, not a homogeneous dependent opacity that clears with treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tension pneumothorax shows an abnormally dark hemithorax without lung markings, not a white opacity.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with heart failure has worsening dyspnea. PA and lateral chest radiographs are shown; the arrow on the lateral film marks the finding of interest. What does this finding indicate?

explanation.summary: Blunting of the normally sharp costophrenic angle with a meniscus of dependent fluid on PA and lateral films is the classic radiographic sign of a pleural effusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blunting of the normally sharp costophrenic angle with a meniscus of dependent fluid on PA and lateral films is the classic radiographic sign of a pleural effusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiomegaly widens the cardiac silhouette beyond half the thoracic width without blunting the costophrenic angles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A hiatal hernia appears as a retrocardiac mass, often with an air-fluid level, behind the heart rather than at the lateral costophrenic angle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lobar pneumonia appears as dense consolidation with air bronchograms within a lobe, not dependent fluid with a meniscus at the costophrenic angle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pneumothorax shows a thin visceral pleural line with absent lung markings beyond it; free air rises and does not form a dependent meniscus.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old retired pipefitter has chest pain, weight loss, and dyspnea. A coronal chest CT is shown (arrows and circle). What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Nodular, circumferential pleural thickening that encases the lung with effusion is the classic CT appearance of malignant mesothelioma, strongly associated with asbestos exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nodular, circumferential pleural thickening that encases the lung with effusion is the classic CT appearance of malignant mesothelioma, strongly associated with asbestos exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A bulla is a thin-walled air space larger than 1 cm, lucent rather than soft-tissue dense.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lobar pneumonia consolidates lung parenchyma with air bronchograms rather than encasing the lung in nodular pleural thickening.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary embolism is a filling defect within the pulmonary arteries, not a rind of soft tissue encasing the pleura.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sarcoidosis shows hilar adenopathy and perilymphatic nodules; circumferential pleural rind is not typical.

questions.stem: These circled lesions were found on the parietal pleura at autopsy of a 75-year-old retired insulation worker. They are a hallmark of remote exposure to which agent?

explanation.summary: Discrete, ivory-white collagenous plaques on the parietal and diaphragmatic pleura are the classic gross marker of prior asbestos exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Discrete, ivory-white collagenous plaques on the parietal and diaphragmatic pleura are the classic gross marker of prior asbestos exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cigarette smoke damages airways and parenchyma but does not cause parietal pleural plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coal dust produces anthracotic macules and nodules in the lung, not white fibrous pleural plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radiation can cause pleural thickening and fibrosis, but discrete pearly-white plaques on the parietal pleura are the signature of asbestos.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tuberculosis can cause diffuse pleural thickening or calcification after effusion or empyema, typically unilateral and not discrete plaques.

questions.stem: This cross-sectioned lung is from a 72-year-old former shipyard worker with progressive dyspnea and chest pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A rind of tumor encasing the entire lung and encroaching on fissures is the characteristic gross appearance of diffuse malignant pleural mesothelioma.
explanation.whyCorrect: A rind of tumor encasing the entire lung and encroaching on fissures is the characteristic gross appearance of diffuse malignant pleural mesothelioma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchogenic adenocarcinoma usually forms a discrete peripheral mass rather than a diffuse rind encasing the entire lung.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lobar pneumonia consolidates a lobe without a thick, firm pleural-based tumor encasing it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A pulmonary infarct is a wedge-shaped, hemorrhagic, pleural-based lesion, not a circumferential sheath.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sarcoidosis produces small nodules and hilar adenopathy, not a thick tumor rind around the lung.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has dyspnea after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. His chest radiograph and coronal CT are shown. What injury do they indicate?

explanation.summary: Displacement of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity through a defect in the diaphragm indicates traumatic diaphragmatic rupture, which most often affects the left hemidiaphragm and requires surgical repair.
explanation.whyCorrect: Displacement of abdominal contents into the thoracic cavity through a defect in the diaphragm indicates traumatic diaphragmatic rupture, which most often affects the left hemidiaphragm and requires surgical repair.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A hiatal hernia moves the stomach through the esophageal hiatus in the midline, without loss of the diaphragmatic contour after trauma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lobar collapse shows dense lung with volume loss, not abdominal viscera above a disrupted diaphragm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A loculated empyema is a lenticular fluid collection with an enhancing pleural rind, not herniated bowel.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tension pneumothorax produces a hyperlucent hemithorax with mediastinal shift, not bowel in the chest.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man develops severe hypoxemia and bilateral infiltrates 2 days after aspiration pneumonia and dies despite ventilation. A lung section is shown; the arrow marks a key feature. What underlying process does this represent?

explanation.summary: ARDS is the clinical correlate of diffuse alveolar damage, characterized by alveolar epithelial and endothelial injury, protein-rich exudate, and inflammatory infiltration of airspaces.
explanation.whyCorrect: ARDS is the clinical correlate of diffuse alveolar damage, characterized by alveolar epithelial and endothelial injury, protein-rich exudate, and inflammatory infiltration of airspaces.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchopneumonia is a patchy neutrophilic exudate centered on bronchioles; abscesses show liquefactive necrosis, not diffuse damage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Caseating granulomas are nodules of epithelioid histiocytes with central necrosis, as in TB, not diffuse septal widening with hemorrhage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Emphysema destroys and thins alveolar walls, enlarging airspaces, rather than widening septa with exudate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UIP is a chronic, patchy fibrosis with honeycombing and fibroblastic foci, not an acute exudative injury.

questions.stem: A newborn delivered at 29 weeks' gestation develops grunting, nasal flaring, and retractions within hours of birth and is intubated. The chest radiograph is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Diffuse ground-glass opacity with air bronchograms and underinflated lungs in a preterm infant is the classic surfactant-deficiency (RDS) pattern.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diffuse ground-glass opacity with air bronchograms and underinflated lungs in a preterm infant is the classic surfactant-deficiency (RDS) pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A normal neonatal chest has clear lungs with normal volumes and no diffuse ground-glass opacity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia shows bowel loops in the chest, usually left-sided, with mediastinal shift.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Meconium aspiration affects term or post-term infants and shows patchy, coarse opacities with hyperinflation, not low volumes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tension pneumothorax shows a hyperlucent hemithorax with mediastinal shift, not bilateral ground-glass.

questions.stem: This lung section is from a neonate born at 28 weeks' gestation who died of progressive respiratory distress. What are the pink structures lining the airspaces (arrow)?

explanation.summary: Surfactant deficiency causes alveolar collapse, epithelial injury, and plasma leak that forms eosinophilic hyaline membranes lining alveoli in neonatal RDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Surfactant deficiency causes alveolar collapse, epithelial injury, and plasma leak that forms eosinophilic hyaline membranes lining alveoli in neonatal RDS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid forms amorphous extracellular deposits with apple-green birefringence on Congo red, not linear ductal membranes in neonates.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bronchial cartilage plates are basophilic hyaline cartilage in larger airway walls, not eosinophilic linings of alveolar ducts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granulomas are nodular collections of epithelioid macrophages, not thin linear membranes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Psammoma bodies are concentric laminated calcifications in papillary tumors, not membranes lining alveolar ducts.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has sudden pleuritic chest pain and tachypnea 10 days after hip surgery. This contrast-enhanced CT of the chest is obtained; the arrows mark the abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: On CT pulmonary angiography, hypodense (dark) filling defects within the contrast-opacified pulmonary arteries indicate thromboemboli. Large central emboli can cause hyperventilation and a secondary respiratory alkalosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: On CT pulmonary angiography, hypodense (dark) filling defects within the contrast-opacified pulmonary arteries indicate thromboemboli. Large central emboli can cause hyperventilation and a secondary respiratory alkalosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Aortic dissection shows an intimal flap separating true and false lumens in the aorta, not filling defects within the pulmonary arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A lung abscess is a cavitary parenchymal lesion, often with an air-fluid level, rather than a filling defect inside contrast-filled pulmonary arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enlarged lymph nodes are soft-tissue masses outside the vessels in the mediastinum or hila; they may compress but do not fill the arterial lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pericardial effusion appears as fluid density surrounding the heart within the pericardial sac, not as defects within the central pulmonary arteries.
